U.S. House Elections

Elections to the U.S. Senate happened on November 3, 2026. Thirty-three of the 100 seats in the chamber were up for election and another two seats were up for special election.

Of the 33 regularly scheduled general elections in 2026, Democrats controlled 13 and Republicans controlled 20.

In the 2026 general elections, Democrats needed to gain a net of four seats to win a majority in the chamber. Meanwhile, Republicans could only lose two seats and retain a majority in the chamber.

As of Sept. 3, 2026, 11 U.S. Senate incumbents — four Democrats and seven Republicans — were not running for re-election in 2026.

Ballotpedia followed 12 seats as battleground races in 2026. Democrats controlled three of those seats, and Republicans controlled nine.

Democrats were defending two seats in states that Donald Trump (R) won in the 2024 presidential election. Those states were Georgia and Michigan. Republicans were defending one seat in a state that Kamala Harris (D) won in the 2024 presidential election. That state was Maine.

Two special elections also happened on November 3, 2026. One special election was to fill the last two years of the six-year term that Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) was elected to in 2022. The other special election was to fill the last two years of the six-year term that J.D. Vance (R-Ohio) was elected to in 2022.

As a result of the 2024 general elections, Republicans won a 53-45 majority in the chamber. Additionally, two independents caucus with the Democrats. Heading into the 2024 general election, Democrats had a 47-49 majority with four independents. Three of those independents caucused with the Democrats, and one other counted towards the Democratic majority for committee purposes. Democrats could not lose any seats and retain a majority in the chamber. Meanwhile, Republicans needed to gain a net of two seats and retain a majority in the chamber. In the 2024 general elections, Republicans gained a net of four seats.

Four incumbents — all Democrats — lost re-election in the general elections in 2024.

Those elected to the U.S. Senate in the regularly scheduled elections on November 3, 2026, will begin their six-year terms on January 3, 2027.

Election results, 2026

See also: Election results, 2026: U.S. Senate

As of 4:00 PM ET on Nov. 6, 2026, Democrats had won 20 and Republicans 13 of the 35 U.S. Senate races. Two remain uncalled (zero previously held by Democrats, two by Republicans). Seven changed party control (seven to Democrats, zero to Republicans).

As of 4:00 PM ET on Nov. 6, 2026, Decision Desk HQ projected that Democrats would win control of the U.S. Senate.[1]

Heading into the November 3, 2026, election, 35 of 100 U.S. Senate seats were up for election. Thirty-three of those seats were up for regular election, and two were up for special elections.

Republicans held a 53-47 majority in the U.S. Senate. Democrats’ 47 seats included two independents who caucus with Democrats. Democrats were defending two U.S. Senate seats in states Donald Trump (R) won in the 2024 presidential election. Republicans were defending one U.S. Senate seat in a state Kamala Harris (D) won in 2024.

Of the seats up for election in 2026, Democrats hold 13 and Republicans hold 22. Eleven members of the U.S. Senate are not running for re-election, more than in any year since 2012.

Ballotpedia identified 13 races (37.1%) as general election battlegrounds in 2026. Democrats hold three of those seats, and Republicans hold 10.

Eleven seats were open because the incumbent did not run for re-election. Ten incumbents retired from public office and one incumbent ran for another office. Click here to learn more.

Ballotpedia does not include incumbents who leave office early or lose re-election in a primary in our analysis of incumbents not running for re-election. For more information about incumbents who left office early, announced resignations, or lost primaries, click here.

Cook Partisan Voter Index

The Cook Political Report's Partisan Voter Index (PVI) is a measurement tool that scores each congressional district based on how strongly it leans toward one political party. The index, developed by Charles Cook of the The Cook Political Report (CPR), compares each congressional district's score to that of the nation as a whole. According to Politico, the PVI is designed to "provide a quick overall assessment of generic partisan strength in a congressional district."[23][24][25]

The data in the report is compiled by POLIDATA, a political data analysis company, with assistance from National Journal and The Cook Political Report.[26][27]

Statistics:

  • 204 districts had a PVI that leaned Democratic
  • 231 districts had a PVI that leaned Republican
  • Pennsylvania's 3rd Congressional District was the most Democratic district with a PVI of D+40.
  • Alabama's 4th Congressional District was the most Republican district with a PVI of R+33.

Prediction markets

See also: Prediction markets

A prediction market is a platform where users buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events. The price of a contract reflects the market's estimated probability of that outcome — a contract priced at 55 cents suggests the market estimates a 55 percent chance the event occurs. Volume reflects how actively a market is being traded.[28] Unlike polls, which survey a sample of voters, prediction markets aggregate the financial stakes of individual bettors. A market with higher trading volume is generally considered more reliable than one with low volume, though prices can be influenced by large individual traders.

This section displays the contract prices on the outcome of this election from Kalshi, one of several prediction market platforms. Ballotpedia displays prediction market data for informational purposes; these markets do not predict election outcomes with certainty.[29]

Elections to the U.S. House of Representatives happened on November 3, 2026. All 435 districts were up for election. Five of the chamber's six non-voting members were also up for election.

Democrats needed to gain a net of three districts to win a majority in the chamber in the 2026 elections. Meanwhile, Republicans could lose no more than two districts to retain a majority in the chamber.

Sixty U.S. House incumbents — 23 Democrats and 37 Republicans — were not running for re-election in 2026.

Ballotpedia identified 46 districts (12%) as battleground races in 2026. Democrats held 25 of those districts, and Republicans held 21.

There were 21 Democratic-held U.S. House districts up for election in 2026 that Donald Trump (R) won in the 2024 presidential election. Conversely, there were nine Republican-held U.S. House districts up for election in 2026 that Kamala Harris (D) won in the 2024 presidential election.

As a result of the 2024 general elections, Republicans gained a 220-215 majority in the chamber. Heading into the general elections, Republicans had a 220-212 majority with three vacancies. Two vacancies happened because Democratic members died, and one happened because a Republican member left office early.

In 2024, Democrats needed to retain control of the two vacant seats and gain a net of four seats to win a majority. They retained control of both seats and gained a net of one seat. For Republicans, retaining control required limiting their losses to no more than three seats, including the vacant seat.

On the Ballot Episode 222 - How Many House Seats Could Flip as a Result of Redistricting Efforts Around the Country?

Eleven incumbents — four Democrats and seven Republicans — lost re-election in the general elections. ​​Additionally, four incumbents — two Democrats and two Republicans — lost re-election in the primary elections.

As of July 26, 2026, six states — California, Florida, Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Texas — used different congressional maps for the 2026 election than they did in 2024 because they voluntarily underwent mid-decade redistricting. Additionally, Ohio used a different map due to state law, and Alabama, Louisiana, and Utah did so due to litigation.

Those elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in the regularly scheduled elections on November 3, 2026, will begin their two-year terms on January 3, 2027.

Election results, 2026

See also: Election results, 2026: U.S. House

As of 4:00 PM ET on Nov. 6, 2026, Democrats had won 250 and Republicans 157 of the 435 U.S. House races. Twenty-eight remain uncalled (six previously held by Democrats, 22 by Republicans). Forty-five changed party control (43 to Democrats, two to Republicans).

As of 4:00 PM ET on Nov. 6, 2026, Decision Desk HQ projected that Democrats would win control of the U.S. House.[1]

Heading into the November 3, 2026, election, all 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives were up for election. Five of the chamber’s six non-voting members were also up for election.

Republicans held a 218-214 majority in the U.S. House, with one independent who caucuses with Republicans and two vacancies. Democrats were defending 22 districts that Donald Trump (R) won in the 2024 presidential election. Republicans were defending eight districts that Kamala Harris (D) won in 2024.

Ballotpedia identified 50 races (11.5%) as general election battlegrounds in 2026. Democrats held 27 of those seats, and Republicans held 23.

Nine states used different congressional maps than they did in 2024. Five states voluntarily redrew their maps mid-decade: California, Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Texas. Ohio adopted a new map because of state law. Alabama, Louisiana, and Utah adopted new maps because of litigation.

Sixty incumbents did not seek re-election. Thirty-two incumbents retired from public office, and 28 ran for other offices. Click here to learn more.

Ballotpedia does not include incumbents who leave office early or lose re-election in a primary in our analysis of incumbents not running for re-election. Eleven House incumbents have lost re-election in primaries this year. For more information about incumbents who left office early, announced resignations, or lost primaries, click here.

Cook Partisan Voter Index

The Cook Political Report's Partisan Voter Index (PVI) is a measurement tool that scores each congressional district based on how strongly it leans toward one political party. The index, developed by Charles Cook of the The Cook Political Report (CPR), compares each congressional district's score to that of the nation as a whole. According to Politico, the PVI is designed to "provide a quick overall assessment of generic partisan strength in a congressional district."[87][88][89]

The data in the report is compiled by POLIDATA, a political data analysis company, with assistance from National Journal and The Cook Political Report.[90][91]

Statistics:

  • 204 districts had a PVI that leaned Democratic
  • 231 districts had a PVI that leaned Republican
  • Pennsylvania's 3rd Congressional District was the most Democratic district with a PVI of D+40.
  • Alabama's 4th Congressional District was the most Republican district with a PVI of R+33.

Prediction markets

See also: Prediction markets

A prediction market is a platform where users buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events. The price of a contract reflects the market's estimated probability of that outcome — a contract priced at 55 cents suggests the market estimates a 55 percent chance the event occurs. Volume reflects how actively a market is being traded.[95] Unlike polls, which survey a sample of voters, prediction markets aggregate the financial stakes of individual bettors. A market with higher trading volume is generally considered more reliable than one with low volume, though prices can be influenced by large individual traders.

This section displays the contract prices on the outcome of this election from Kalshi, one of several prediction market platforms. Ballotpedia displays prediction market data for informational purposes; these markets do not predict election outcomes with certainty.[96]
